title: Cap. VIII: Inhering vice may oppose liberating justice
pass_a_gloss: What blocks us from setting an inhering vice — taken as what makes us guilty and fit for penalty — opposite the justice that releases us from that guilt and penalty? The greatest writers, Placeus notes, have already judged that way. Nothing blocks it; the opposition itself presses for it. κρίμα comes out of justice; δώρημα comes out of grace. Justice pays each person only what is already his; grace hands over what was not ours before, but someone else's.
pass_b_english: For what forbids an inhering vice, insofar as it makes us guilty and worthy of penalty, from being set opposite that justice which frees us from that guilt and penalty — as we have seen the greatest men judged? Not only does nothing forbid it; that very opposition requires it. For κρίμα is from justice, δώρημα from grace. Justice assigns to each only what is his own; grace gives what was otherwise not ours, but another's.
source_text: Quid enim prohibet, vitium inhaerens quatenus nos facit reos & poena dignos ei justitiae opponi, quae nos ab eo reatu & poena liberat, uti vidimus censuisse maximos viros? Id non modo nihil prohibet, sed ipsa illa oppositio exigit. Est enim κρίμα ex justitia, δώρημα ex gratia. Justitia nonnisi suum cuique tribuit; gratia donat id quod alioqui nostrum non erat, sed alienum.
